name: H2 Chemistry
constants: Avogadro constant L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ · Faraday constant F = 9.65 × 10⁴ C mol⁻¹ · Gas constant R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ · Molar volume of gas at r.t.p. = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ · Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K · Specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ · 0 °C = 273 K

questions.q: How many neutrons are in one ³⁷Cl⁻ ion? (proton number of Cl = 17)
questions.x: Neutrons = nucleon number − proton number = 37 − 17 = 20. The extra electron changes the electron count (18), not the neutron count.

questions.q: What is the electronic configuration of Fe³⁺? (proton number of Fe = 26)
questions.x: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². The 4s electrons are lost first, then one 3d electron, leaving [Ar] 3d⁵.

questions.q: Which Period 3 element has a lower first ionisation energy than the element just before it?
questions.x: Al's outermost electron is in a 3p orbital, higher in energy and better shielded by the 3s² electrons than Mg's 3s electron, so it is easier to remove. (S is the other exception, because of paired-electron repulsion in 3p⁴.)

questions.q: The first five ionisation energies of element X are 578, 1817, 2745, 11577 and 14842 kJ mol⁻¹. Which group is X in?
questions.x: The large jump is between the 3rd and 4th ionisation energies, so X has 3 valence electrons and the 4th comes from an inner shell. X is in Group 13 (these are aluminium's values).

questions.q: A beam of ¹H⁺ ions is deflected by +8° in an electric field. Under the same conditions, what is the angle of deflection of ⁶Li³⁺ ions?
questions.x: Deflection is proportional to charge/mass. For ¹H⁺, q/m = 1/1; for ⁶Li³⁺, q/m = 3/6 = 1/2. So the angle is ½ × 8° = +4°, in the same direction because both are positive.

questions.q: What is the shape of an NH₃ molecule?
questions.x: N has 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair. The four electron pairs are arranged tetrahedrally, but the shape (atoms only) is trigonal pyramidal.

questions.q: Which molecule is polar?
questions.x: PCl₃ is trigonal pyramidal (one lone pair on P), so the bond dipoles don't cancel. CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar) and CCl₄ (tetrahedral) are symmetrical, so their dipoles cancel.

questions.q: Why does HF have a much higher boiling point than HCl?
o: HF molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other.
The H–F bond is stronger than the H–Cl bond.
HF has more electrons, so its instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces are stronger.
questions.x: Boiling separates molecules; it doesn't break covalent bonds. F is small and highly electronegative, so HF forms strong hydrogen bonds between molecules. HCl actually has more electrons than HF, so dispersion forces alone would predict the opposite order.

questions.q: What is the shape of the ICl₄⁻ ion?
questions.x: I has 7 valence electrons + 1 for the negative charge = 8. Four are used in I–Cl bonds, leaving 2 lone pairs: 6 electron pairs in total, arranged octahedrally. With the lone pairs opposite each other, the shape is square planar.

questions.q: Which species has the largest bond angle?
questions.x: NO₂⁺ (O=N⁺=O) has two bonding regions and no lone pairs on N, so it is linear, 180°. NH₄⁺ is 109.5°, NH₃ about 107° (1 lone pair) and NH₂⁻ about 104.5° (2 lone pairs).

questions.q: State the hybridisation of each carbon atom in ethene, C₂H₄.
questions.x: Each carbon has three σ bonds (two C–H, one C–C) and no lone pairs, so it is sp² hybridised. The unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to form the π bond.

questions.q: Which is NOT an assumption of the kinetic theory for an ideal gas?
o: All the gas molecules move at the same speed.
The volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the container.
There are no intermolecular forces between the molecules.
Collisions between molecules are perfectly elastic.
questions.x: Molecules in an ideal gas have a distribution of speeds (the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution). Negligible molecular volume, no intermolecular forces and elastic collisions are all assumptions.

questions.q: Under which conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas?
questions.x: At low pressure the molecules are far apart, so their own volume is negligible. At high temperature they move fast enough that intermolecular attractions hardly matter.

questions.q: Which gas deviates most from ideal behaviour at room temperature and pressure?
questions.x: NH₃ molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, so intermolecular attractions are much stronger than in He, H₂ or N₂, which have only weak instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces.

questions.q: 0.20 mol of an ideal gas is held at 300 K in a 4.0 dm³ container. Calculate its pressure. Give your answer in kPa.
questions.x: p = nRT/V = (0.20 × 8.31 × 300) / (4.0 × 10⁻³ m³) = 1.25 × 10⁵ Pa = 125 kPa. Remember to convert dm³ to m³.

questions.q: 0.50 g of a volatile liquid is vaporised and occupies 150 cm³ at 100 °C and 101 kPa. What is its relative molecular mass?
How many moles of NaOH are in 4.0 g of NaOH? (Mr = 40)
questions.x: n = mass / Mr = 4.0 / 40 = 0.10 mol.

questions.q: 10.0 g of CaCO₃ (Mr = 100) reacts with excess dilute HCl. What volume of CO₂ is produced at r.t.p.?
questions.x: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. 0.100 mol CaCO₃ gives 0.100 mol CO₂, and 0.100 × 24.0 = 2.4 dm³.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of aqueous Na₂CO₃ needs 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl for complete reaction to CO₂. What is the concentration of the Na₂CO₃?
questions.x: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. n(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol, so n(Na₂CO₃) = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol, and 1.00 × 10⁻³ / 0.0250 = 0.0400 mol dm⁻³. Forgetting the 1 : 2 ratio gives 0.0800.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of an acidified Fe²⁺ solution reacts exactly with 20.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄. What is the concentration of Fe²⁺? (MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O)

10 cm³ of a gaseous hydrocarbon is burned in excess oxygen. On cooling to room temperature the volume decreases by 25 cm³. Passing the remaining gas through aqueous KOH decreases the volume by a further 30 cm³. What is the hydrocarbon?
questions.x: CO₂ absorbed by KOH = 30 cm³, so x = 3. For CₓHᵧ + (x + y/4)O₂ → xCO₂ + (y/2)H₂O(l), the contraction is 10(1 + y/4) = 25, so y = 6. The hydrocarbon is C₃H₆.

questions.q: Which substance has a standard enthalpy change of formation of zero?
questions.x: ΔHf° is zero only for an element in its standard state. Oxygen's standard state is O₂(g); carbon's is graphite, not diamond. O₃ and H₂O are not standard-state elements.

questions.q: When 0.0250 mol of an acid is neutralised in 50.0 g of water, the temperature rises by 6.0 K. What is the enthalpy change of neutralisation?
questions.x: q = mcΔT = 50.0 × 4.18 × 6.0 = 1254 J. ΔH = −1254 / 0.0250 = −50 200 J mol⁻¹ = −50.2 kJ mol⁻¹. It is negative because the temperature rose (exothermic).

questions.q: Use these standard enthalpy changes of combustion to find ΔHf° of methane: C(graphite) −394, H₂(g) −286, CH₄(g) −890 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.x: ΔHf = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products) = [−394 + 2(−286)] − (−890) = −966 + 890 = −76 kJ mol⁻¹. Forgetting the 2 for H₂ gives +210.

questions.q: Bond energies: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)?
questions.x: ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed = (436 + 242) − 2(431) = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: For CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH° = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Above what temperature does the reaction become spontaneous?
questions.x: Spontaneous when ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0, i.e. T > ΔH/ΔS = 178 000 / 161 = 1106 K. Not converting kJ to J gives 1.11 K.

questions.q: Which compound has the most exothermic lattice energy?
questions.x: Lattice energy is proportional to (q⁺ × q⁻)/(r⁺ + r⁻). MgO has 2+ and 2− ions that are both small, so its lattice energy is far more exothermic than the others.

questions.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
o: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
It makes the reaction more exothermic.
It increases the kinetic energy of the particles.
It shifts the position of equilibrium to the right.
questions.x: A catalyst offers a different route with lower Ea, so more collisions have enough energy to react. ΔH, particle energies and the equilibrium position are unchanged.

questions.q: The rate equation is rate = k[A][B]², with concentrations in mol dm⁻³ and rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. What are the units of k?
questions.x: k = rate / ([A][B]²) = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) / (mol dm⁻³)³ = mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹. A third-order reaction always has these units.

questions.q: Initial rates for A + B → products: [A] 0.10, [B] 0.10 gives rate r; [A] 0.20, [B] 0.10 gives 4r; [A] 0.10, [B] 0.30 gives 3r. What is the rate equation?
questions.x: Doubling [A] quadruples the rate, so second order in A. Tripling [B] triples the rate, so first order in B. Rate = k[A]²[B].

questions.q: A first-order reaction leaves 25% of the reactant after 60 minutes. What is its half-life? Give your answer in minutes.
questions.x: 100% → 50% → 25% is two half-lives, so t½ = 60 / 2 = 30 min. A first-order reaction has a constant half-life.

questions.q: For (CH₃)₃CBr + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃COH + Br⁻, rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr]. Which statement is correct?
o: Doubling both concentrations doubles the rate.
OH⁻ takes part in the rate-determining step.
The reaction is second order overall.
questions.x: The rate depends only on [(CH₃)₃CBr], so doubling both doubles the rate. OH⁻ does not appear in the rate equation, so it reacts after the slow step (SN1) and the reaction is first order overall.

questions.q: Propanone reacts with iodine in acid, with propanone and H⁺ in large excess. A graph of [I₂] against time is a straight line sloping down. What is the order with respect to I₂?
o: It cannot be found from this graph.
questions.x: A straight line on a concentration–time graph means the rate (the gradient) stays constant as [I₂] falls, so the rate doesn't depend on [I₂]: zero order. Excess propanone and H⁺ keep their concentrations effectively constant.

questions.q: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Which change increases the equilibrium yield of NH₃?
questions.x: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (2 vs 4), so the yield rises. Higher temperature favours the endothermic backward reaction; a catalyst doesn't move the equilibrium.

questions.q: What are the units of Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
questions.x: Kc = [NH₃]² / ([N₂][H₂]³), so the units are (mol dm⁻³)² / (mol dm⁻³)⁴ = (mol dm⁻³)⁻² = mol⁻² dm⁶.

questions.q: 1.0 mol H₂ and 1.0 mol I₂ are heated in a 1.0 dm³ flask. At equilibrium there is 1.6 mol HI. What is Kc for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI?
questions.x: Forming 1.6 mol HI uses 0.8 mol each of H₂ and I₂, leaving 0.2 mol of each. Kc = 1.6² / (0.2 × 0.2) = 2.56 / 0.04 = 64. Forgetting to square [HI] gives 40.

questions.q: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). At a total pressure of 1.0 atm, N₂O₄ is 50% dissociated. What is Kp?
questions.x: From 1 mol N₂O₄: 0.5 mol N₂O₄ and 1.0 mol NO₂, 1.5 mol total. Partial pressures are 1/3 atm and 2/3 atm. Kp = (2/3)² / (1/3) = 4/3 = 1.33 atm. Using moles instead of partial pressures gives 2.0.

questions.q: The forward reaction of an equilibrium is exothermic. What happens to Kc when the temperature is raised?
o: Kc increases at first, then returns to its original value.
questions.x: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic (backward) reaction, so the equilibrium mixture has less product and Kc falls. Only temperature changes the value of K.

questions.q: What is the conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻?
questions.x: A conjugate base has one H⁺ fewer than its acid: H₂PO₄⁻ → HPO₄²⁻ + H⁺. H₃PO₄ is its conjugate acid.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq)?
questions.x: HCl is a strong acid and fully ionises, so [H⁺] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³ and pH = −log(0.010) = 2.0.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.050 mol dm⁻³ Ba(OH)₂(aq) at 298 K?
questions.x: Each Ba(OH)₂ gives 2 OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ and pOH = 1.0. pH = 14.0 − 1.0 = 13.0. Forgetting the 2 gives 12.7.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid? (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³)
questions.x: [H⁺] = √(Ka × c) = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = 1.34 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, so pH = 2.87. pH 1.00 treats it as a strong acid; 4.74 is pKa.

questions.q: A buffer contains 0.20 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COONa. What is its pH? (pKa of CH₃COOH = 4.74)
questions.x: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = 4.74 + log(0.10/0.20) = 4.74 − 0.30 = 4.44. Putting the ratio upside down gives 5.04.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH is titrated with 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. What is the pH at the equivalence point? (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³)
questions.x: At equivalence the total volume is 50.0 cm³, so [CH₃COO⁻] = 0.050. Kb = Kw/Ka = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰, [OH⁻] = √(5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.050) = 5.3 × 10⁻⁶, pOH = 5.28, pH = 8.72. Forgetting the dilution gives 8.87.

questions.q: Which indicator is most suitable for titrating ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide?
questions.x: A weak acid–strong base titration has an equivalence point above pH 7 and a steep section roughly from pH 7 to 11. Only phenolphthalein changes colour in that range.

questions.q: In a galvanic (electrochemical) cell, where does oxidation take place and what is the sign of that electrode?
o: at the anode, which is negative
at the anode, which is positive
at the cathode, which is negative
at the cathode, which is positive
questions.x: Oxidation always happens at the anode. In a galvanic cell the anode releases electrons into the external circuit, so it is the negative electrode. (In electrolysis the anode is positive.)

questions.q: E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V and E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V. What is E°cell for the Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu cell? Give your answer in V.
questions.x: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. Cu²⁺ is reduced and Zn is oxidised.

questions.q: A current of 0.500 A passes through aqueous CuSO₄ for 1930 s. What mass of copper is deposited? (Ar of Cu = 63.5)
questions.x: Q = It = 0.500 × 1930 = 965 C, which is 965 / 96 500 = 0.0100 mol of electrons. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so 0.00500 mol Cu = 0.318 g. Forgetting the 2 electrons gives 0.635 g.

questions.q: E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V. Which species can oxidise Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ under standard conditions? E° values: Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V, I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V.
questions.x: The oxidising agent needs a more positive E° than +0.77 V so that E°cell is positive. Only Cl₂ (+1.36 V) qualifies: E°cell = 1.36 − 0.77 = +0.59 V.

questions.q: In the cell Zn | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu, the Cu²⁺ solution is diluted. What happens to the cell e.m.f.?
o: It decreases, because E(Cu²⁺/Cu) becomes less positive.
It increases, because E(Cu²⁺/Cu) becomes more positive.
It stays the same, because E° values don't depend on concentration.
It decreases, because E(Zn²⁺/Zn) becomes more negative.
questions.x: Lowering [Cu²⁺] shifts Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu to the left, so the copper electrode potential becomes less positive. The difference between the electrodes falls, so Ecell falls. E° is fixed but E is not.

questions.q: E°cell for Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu is +1.10 V. What is ΔG° for this reaction?
How does atomic radius change from Na to Cl across Period 3?
o: It decreases, because nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same.
It increases, because more electrons are added.
It decreases, because more shells are added.
It stays about the same, because all the electrons are in the third shell.
questions.x: Across a period, protons are added but the extra electrons go into the same shell, so shielding barely changes. The rising effective nuclear charge pulls the electrons closer.

questions.q: Which Period 3 oxide dissolves in water to give a solution of about pH 13?
questions.x: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH, a strong alkali (pH about 13). MgO is only sparingly soluble (pH about 9), Al₂O₃ is insoluble, and SO₃ gives H₂SO₄ (pH about 1).

questions.q: Which Period 3 oxide is amphoteric?
questions.x: Al₂O₃ reacts with acids (forming Al³⁺) and with alkalis (forming [Al(OH)₄]⁻). MgO is basic; SiO₂ and P₄O₁₀ are acidic.

questions.q: Which Period 3 chloride dissolves in water to give a solution of pH 7?
questions.x: NaCl simply dissolves into hydrated ions. AlCl₃ gives an acidic solution (pH about 3) because the small, highly charged Al³⁺ polarises water. SiCl₄ and PCl₅ hydrolyse completely to give HCl (pH about 1–2).

questions.q: Element X is in Period 3. Its oxide has a very high melting point, is insoluble in water and doesn't react with dilute acids, but reacts with hot concentrated NaOH. Its chloride is a liquid that fumes in moist air. What is X?
questions.x: SiO₂ is giant covalent (high melting point), acidic, and reacts only with hot concentrated alkali. SiCl₄ is a simple molecular liquid that hydrolyses to give HCl fumes. Al₂O₃ would also react with dilute acid; P's oxides are low-melting.

questions.q: Which is NOT a typical property of transition elements?
questions.x: Transition metals have high melting points because both 3d and 4s electrons take part in strong metallic bonding. Variable oxidation states, coloured ions and catalytic activity are all typical.

questions.q: What is the oxidation state of chromium in K₂Cr₂O₇?
Why is aqueous [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ coloured?
o: Ligands split the 3d orbitals into two energy levels, and an electron absorbs visible light to move to the higher level.
Electrons move from the 3d to the 4s orbital and emit visible light.
The copper ion has a full 3d subshell, which reflects blue light.
Water molecules absorb red light when they bond to the copper ion.
questions.x: In an octahedral complex the 3d orbitals split. Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) has a partly filled subshell, so a d–d transition can absorb light of energy ΔE; the colour seen is the complementary colour of what is absorbed.

questions.q: Which aqueous ion is colourless?
questions.x: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰: the d subshell is full, so no d–d transition is possible. Cu²⁺ (3d⁹), Fe³⁺ (3d⁵) and Ti³⁺ (3d¹) all have partly filled d subshells.

questions.q: Adding concentrated HCl to blue aqueous Cu²⁺ gives a yellow-green solution of [CuCl₄]²⁻. How do the coordination number and shape change?
questions.x: Cl⁻ ligands replace H₂O. Cl⁻ is larger than H₂O, so only four fit around Cu²⁺, and [CuCl₄]²⁻ is tetrahedral.

questions.q: What is the coordination number of nickel in [Ni(H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂)₃]²⁺?
questions.x: Ethane-1,2-diamine is bidentate: each molecule bonds through both N atoms. Three ligands × 2 = 6 dative bonds, so the coordination number is 6.

questions.q: Fe²⁺ catalyses S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂. E° values: S₂O₈²⁻/SO₄²⁻ +2.01 V, Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V, I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V. Why does it work?
o: S₂O₈²⁻ oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, then Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂; both steps have positive E°cell and involve oppositely charged ions.
Fe²⁺ makes the overall reaction more exothermic.
Fe²⁺ reduces S₂O₈²⁻ and is not regenerated, so less I⁻ is needed.
Fe²⁺ provides a surface on which the two anions adsorb.
questions.x: Step 1: E°cell = 2.01 − 0.77 = +1.24 V. Step 2: E°cell = 0.77 − 0.54 = +0.23 V. Fe²⁺ is regenerated, and each step has a cation reacting with an anion, avoiding the repulsion that slows the uncatalysed anion–anion reaction. This is homogeneous catalysis, not surface adsorption.

questions.q: Name the functional group present in CH₃CHO.
questions.x: –CHO is the aldehyde group: a carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one H. CH₃CHO is ethanal.

questions.q: How many structural isomers have the formula C₄H₉Br?
questions.x: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane: 4. (2-bromobutane also has enantiomers, but those are stereoisomers, not structural isomers.)

questions.q: Which compound shows cis–trans isomerism?
questions.x: Each C of the C=C in but-2-ene (CH₃CH=CHCH₃) carries two different groups. In the others, one C of the double bond carries two identical groups (two H or two CH₃).

questions.q: How many stereoisomers does pent-3-en-2-ol, CH₃CH=CHCH(OH)CH₃, have?
questions.x: The C=C gives cis and trans forms, and C2 is a chiral centre (H, OH, CH₃, CH=CHCH₃), giving two enantiomers of each. 2 × 2 = 4.

questions.q: How many stereoisomers does 2,3-dibromobutane, CH₃CHBrCHBrCH₃, have?
questions.x: Two chiral centres would allow 2² = 4, but the molecule is symmetrical: the (R,S) form has an internal mirror plane and is the same as (S,R). That meso form plus the (R,R)/(S,S) pair makes 3.

questions.q: In the reaction of CN⁻ with ethanal, what role does CN⁻ play?
questions.x: CN⁻ donates its lone pair to the electron-deficient carbonyl carbon. It is a nucleophile, and the reaction is nucleophilic addition.

questions.q: What type of reaction occurs between methane and chlorine in ultraviolet light?
questions.x: UV light splits Cl₂ into Cl• radicals, which take an H from CH₄. A Cl atom replaces an H atom: free-radical substitution.

questions.q: Which equation is the initiation step in the chlorination of methane?
questions.x: Initiation creates radicals: UV light breaks the weak Cl–Cl bond homolytically. The next two are propagation steps, and the last is a termination step.

questions.q: How many structural isomers of C₅H₁₁Cl can form when 2-methylbutane reacts with chlorine in UV light?
questions.x: 2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃, has four different kinds of H: on the two equivalent CH₃ groups at C1, on C2, on C3 and on C4. So 4 monochloro structural isomers.

questions.q: What is seen when bromine water is shaken with an alkene?
questions.x: Br₂ adds across the C=C (electrophilic addition), so the orange colour of bromine disappears. Purple to colourless is the test with KMnO₄.

questions.q: What is the major product when HBr reacts with propene?
questions.x: H⁺ adds to the end carbon to give the more stable secondary carbocation CH₃C⁺HCH₃, which Br⁻ then attacks (Markovnikov's rule).

questions.q: 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, is heated with acidified KMnO₄. What are the organic products?
questions.x: Hot acidified KMnO₄ cleaves the C=C. The (CH₃)₂C= end becomes (CH₃)₂C=O, propanone. The =CHCH₃ end becomes CH₃CHO, which is further oxidised to CH₃COOH. The diol forms only with cold dilute KMnO₄.

questions.q: Ethene is bubbled into bromine water containing dissolved sodium chloride. Which product is NOT formed?
questions.x: The first step is always attack by the electrophile Br^δ+, so every product contains Br. The carbocation is then attacked by whichever nucleophile reaches it: Br⁻, H₂O or Cl⁻. A product with no bromine cannot form.

questions.q: Why does benzene usually undergo substitution rather than addition?
o: Substitution keeps the stable delocalised π electron system intact.
Benzene has no π electrons to attack electrophiles.
The C–H bonds in benzene are weaker than C=C bonds.
Addition reactions need a catalyst, and substitution doesn't.
questions.x: Addition would destroy the delocalised ring of six π electrons and lose its extra stability. Substitution replaces an H and restores the delocalised system.

questions.q: Benzene is nitrated with a mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄. Give the formula of the electrophile.
questions.x: H₂SO₄ protonates HNO₃, which loses water: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. The nitronium ion NO₂⁺ is the electrophile.

questions.q: Methylbenzene reacts with chlorine in ultraviolet light. What is the main organic product?
questions.x: UV light gives free-radical substitution on the CH₃ side chain. Substitution on the ring (2- and 4-positions) needs a halogen carrier such as AlCl₃ or FeCl₃ instead.

questions.q: Compared with benzene, how does methylbenzene behave in nitration?
o: It reacts faster, giving mainly 2- and 4-substituted products.
It reacts faster, giving mainly the 3-substituted product.
It reacts slower, giving mainly 2- and 4-substituted products.
It reacts slower, giving mainly the 3-substituted product.
questions.x: The CH₃ group donates electron density to the ring, so it activates the ring to electrophilic attack and directs to the 2- and 4-positions.

questions.q: Which route makes 3-nitrobenzoic acid from methylbenzene in the best yield?
o: Heat with acidified KMnO₄, then nitrate with conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄.
Nitrate with conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄, then heat with acidified KMnO₄.
Nitrate with dilute HNO₃, then heat with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇.
Heat with Cl₂ in UV light, then nitrate with conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄.
questions.x: Oxidising first converts CH₃ (2,4-directing) to COOH, which is 3-directing, so nitration then goes to the 3-position. Nitrating first would put NO₂ at the 2- or 4-position.

questions.q: What is the organic product when bromoethane is heated with aqueous NaOH?
questions.x: In aqueous solution, OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile and replaces Br: CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻ (nucleophilic substitution).

questions.q: What is the main organic product when bromoethane is heated with ethanolic KOH?
questions.x: In ethanol, OH⁻ acts as a base and removes H⁺, giving elimination of HBr to form ethene. Aqueous conditions favour substitution instead.

questions.q: Which halogenoalkane is hydrolysed fastest by water?
questions.x: The rate depends mainly on how easily the C–X bond breaks. C–I is the longest and weakest of these bonds, so iodoalkanes react fastest, even though C–F is the most polar.

questions.q: Which statement about the hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane by OH⁻ is correct?
o: It goes through a carbocation intermediate.
It goes through a single five-coordinate transition state with no intermediate.
It is slower than for 1-bromobutane because the tertiary carbon is crowded.
questions.x: Tertiary halogenoalkanes react by SN1: C–Br breaks first to give a stable tertiary carbocation, which OH⁻ then attacks. The rate depends only on [RBr]. The single transition state describes SN2.

questions.q: Optically active (R)-2-bromobutane is hydrolysed by an SN2 mechanism. What is the product?
o: optically active butan-2-ol with inverted configuration
optically active butan-2-ol with the same configuration
questions.x: In SN2, OH⁻ attacks from the side opposite Br, so the configuration flips (Walden inversion) and a single enantiomer forms. A racemic mixture comes from SN1, where the planar carbocation can be attacked from either face.

questions.q: Why is chlorobenzene not hydrolysed when heated with aqueous NaOH?
o: A lone pair on Cl overlaps with the ring π system, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character.
The C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene is more polar than in chloroethane.
Chlorobenzene is insoluble in water, so it never meets OH⁻.
OH⁻ attacks the ring instead and adds across a C=C bond.
questions.x: Delocalising Cl's lone pair into the ring strengthens the C–Cl bond. The electron-rich ring also repels the incoming nucleophile.

questions.q: Ethanol is heated under reflux with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. What is the organic product and the colour change?
questions.x: Under reflux with excess oxidant, a primary alcohol is fully oxidised to the carboxylic acid. Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) is reduced to Cr³⁺ (green). Distilling the product off as it forms would give ethanal instead.

questions.q: Which alcohol is NOT oxidised by hot acidified K₂Cr₂O₇?
questions.x: 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary: the carbon bearing OH has no H atom to lose, so it isn't oxidised. The others are primary or secondary.

questions.q: Which compound gives a yellow precipitate when warmed with alkaline aqueous iodine?
questions.x: The iodoform (CHI₃) test is positive for CH₃CH(OH)– and CH₃CO– groups. Butan-2-ol is CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. The others lack a CH₃CH(OH)– group.

questions.q: Which compound reacts with aqueous NaOH but does NOT give CO₂ with aqueous Na₂CO₃?
questions.x: Phenol is acidic enough to react with NaOH (its anion is stabilised by delocalisation into the ring), but too weak to react with carbonate. Ethanol doesn't react with NaOH; the carboxylic acids react with both.

questions.q: Phenol reacts with excess bromine water at room temperature. How many moles of Br₂ react with 1 mol of phenol?
questions.x: The OH group strongly activates the ring, so substitution happens at 2, 4 and 6 without a catalyst, forming a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol. That uses 3 Br₂ (and gives 3 HBr).

questions.q: Compound Y, C₇H₈O, gives H₂ with sodium but doesn't react with aqueous NaOH and doesn't decolourise bromine water. What is Y?
questions.x: Reacting with Na means Y has an OH group. Not reacting with NaOH or bromine water rules out a phenol, so the OH is on a side chain: C₆H₅CH₂OH. Methoxybenzene has no OH, so wouldn't react with Na.

questions.q: Which reagent gives an orange precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones?
questions.x: 2,4-DNPH undergoes condensation with any C=O group to give an orange 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone. Tollens', Fehling's and dichromate tests only respond to aldehydes, because ketones are not easily oxidised.

questions.q: Which test distinguishes propanal from propanone?
questions.x: Propanal, an aldehyde, is oxidised and reduces Ag⁺ to a silver mirror. Propanone, a ketone, does not react. Both give an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH.

questions.q: Ethanal reacts with HCN (with a trace of NaCN) to form 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, which has a chiral centre. Why is the product optically inactive?
o: The planar carbonyl group is attacked equally from both faces, giving a racemic mixture.
The product has a plane of symmetry.
The reaction goes through a carbocation that rearranges.
CN⁻ attacks from the side opposite the oxygen, so only one enantiomer forms.
questions.x: The C=O carbon and its three substituents are trigonal planar. CN⁻ is equally likely to attack from above or below, so the two enantiomers form in equal amounts and their rotations cancel.

questions.q: Which compound gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent but no red-brown precipitate with Fehling's solution?
questions.x: Aliphatic aldehydes like ethanal give both tests. Aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde reduce Tollens' reagent but not Fehling's. Ketones give neither.

questions.q: Compound Z, C₄H₈O, gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH and a yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine, but no silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. What is Z?
questions.x: 2,4-DNPH shows a C=O group; no reaction with Tollens' means a ketone; the iodoform test needs CH₃CO–. Only CH₃COCH₂CH₃ fits. But-3-en-2-ol gives iodoform but has no C=O.

questions.q: Ethanoic acid is heated with ethanol and a few drops of concentrated H₂SO₄. Name the organic product.
questions.x: This is esterification (a condensation): CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O. The acid part is named second: ethyl ethanoate.

questions.q: Which is the strongest acid?
questions.x: Electron-withdrawing Cl atoms spread out the negative charge on the carboxylate ion and stabilise it, so two Cl atoms give the strongest acid. Alkyl groups donate electrons and weaken the acid.

questions.q: Put these in order of ease of hydrolysis, easiest first: CH₃COCl, CH₃CH₂Cl, C₆H₅Cl.
questions.x: In an acyl chloride the carbon is bonded to both O and Cl, so it is very electron-deficient and reacts with cold water. Chloroalkanes need heating with NaOH(aq). Chlorobenzene's C–Cl bond is strengthened by delocalisation, so it barely hydrolyses.

questions.q: What are the products when ethyl propanoate is heated under reflux with aqueous NaOH?
questions.x: Alkaline hydrolysis of CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃ gives the carboxylate salt of the acid part, CH₃CH₂COO⁻Na⁺, and the alcohol part, ethanol. Acid hydrolysis would give the free carboxylic acid.

questions.q: Phenyl ethanoate, CH₃COOC₆H₅, is heated with excess aqueous NaOH. How many moles of NaOH react with 1 mol of the ester?
questions.x: Hydrolysis gives CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ and phenol. Phenol is acidic and reacts with a second NaOH to form sodium phenoxide, so 2 mol of NaOH are used.

questions.q: Which reagents convert nitrobenzene into phenylamine?
o: tin and concentrated HCl, then NaOH(aq)
LiAlH₄ in dry ether, then H₂O
NH₃ in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube
questions.x: Sn/conc. HCl reduces –NO₂ to –NH₃⁺; NaOH is then added to release the free amine. Concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄ is the nitrating mixture.

questions.q: Which shows ethylamine, ammonia and phenylamine in order of decreasing base strength?
questions.x: The ethyl group donates electrons, making the N lone pair more available to accept H⁺. In phenylamine the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, making it less available.

questions.q: Why is ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂, almost neutral rather than basic?
o: The lone pair on N is delocalised over the C=O group.
The N atom has no lone pair.
The C=O group donates electrons to the N atom.
questions.x: The N lone pair overlaps with the π system of the neighbouring C=O, and the electronegative O draws electron density away. The lone pair is much less available to accept a proton.

questions.q: What is the organic product when ethanoyl chloride reacts with ethylamine?
questions.x: This is a condensation (nucleophilic acyl substitution): the amine N attacks the carbonyl carbon and HCl is lost, forming an amide link.

questions.q: In which form does glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, mainly exist in a solution of pH 1?
questions.x: At very low pH there is plenty of H⁺, so both the amine group (protonated to –NH₃⁺) and the carboxylate (as –COOH) carry H. The zwitterion dominates near the isoelectric point, and the anion at high pH.

questions.q: How many different tripeptides can be made that each contain one glycine, one alanine and one serine residue?
questions.x: A peptide has a direction (N-terminus to C-terminus), so each order is a different molecule: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6. 27 would allow amino acids to repeat.
